newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania's central bank ignores IMF concerns.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania's central bank ignores IMF concerns.

text.p: The Bank of Tanzania will push ahead with controversial plans to cut its Statutary Minimum Reserve (SMR) to commercial banks by 50 percent despite concerns raised by the IMF, a senior central bank official said.

"As of now there are no plans to change or amend the circular. No review has been done and we are proceeding with the implementation process so as to enforce it by January 20," the official in BoT's bank supervision department told Reuters.

The surprise decision by the BoT was made without informing or consulting the IMF (International Monetary Fund) which has protested the issue and warned the BoT that cutting the SMR could fuel monetary policies aimed at reducing inflation, according to senior banking sources and Western embassies.
The BoT's December 17 circular to commercial banks said the SMR would be cut to 6.0 percent from 12 percent in an attempt to boost liquidity for the local commercial banks.
Implementation of the decision is due on Monday, a day before Tanzania meets its major international donors at a Paris Club meeting.
The Paris Club will discuss debt relief for Tanzania worth more than $200 million at the one-day meeting Paris.

"The policy decision is wrong and the timing is wrong. It's bad management on the side of the BoT," an economic analyst told Reuters. "Surely the donors are not stupid, they are going to ask Tanzania why they are doing this," he said.

The analyst, who asked not to be named, said that while the political leadership had made great progress in stabilising its macroeconomic policies, the BoT leadership was making a wrong decision by cutting the SMR.

"It's wrong in the sense that if you want the banks to increase its deposit rates the banks need to make more profits which most commonly is done through increasing the sale of central bank liquidity bills to the commercial banks," he said.
A foreign banking source said the management of the BoT was acting in such an uncoordinated manner that even the treasury had not been consulted on the issue.
"The IMF is not very happy about that whole thing," the foreign banking source told Reuters.

But another official at the central bank defended the decision by arguing that if the liquidity of the commercial banks was not improved it could lead to a situation causing a drop in private investment.
"We are a little bit concerned that the commercial banks are not improving savings and we would not be happy to see savings decline because that could lead to less investments," he said.
After a four-year hiatus, the IMF restored support to Tanzania last November with the approval of a $234 million Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) loan programme.

The first disbursement of the three-year loan followed shortly after the November 8 approval by the Washington-based Fund's executive board and a high-level mission from the IMF is scheduled to arrive for a mid-term review in February.
